title: Satisficing vs Quiet Quitting
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: After a talk left listeners thinking he was endorsing "quiet quitting," Stuart uses this post to clarify what he actually means by satisficing - a term he borrows from Nobel laureate Herbert Simon. Satisficing means meeting a task's basic requirements while deliberately sacrificing additional polish, but the point, he stresses, is not to satisfice everything; it's to satisfice the many low-stakes tasks on your plate precisely so you can pour maximal effort into the handful of tasks that actually matter. He illustrates with concrete teacher examples: glancing past 95% of inbox emails, not chasing every point on a hyper-detailed evaluation rubric, and not letting a hallway interruption derail a lesson's central purpose. The piece reframes satisficing as a discipline of triage rather than a license for mediocrity, positioning it as close to the core thesis of his whole body of work.
points: Distinguishes satisficing sharply from quiet quitting: the goal is to sacrifice quality on low-stakes tasks specifically in order to maximize effort on the few that matter most, not to coast across the board.
Credits Herbert Simon's original 1950s coinage of the term, grounding a personal productivity philosophy in established decision theory.
Gives three concrete, low-stakes teacher examples worth satisficing - most inbox email, full mastery of an evaluation rubric, and minor lesson interruptions - to make the abstract idea actionable.
Frames "knowing which things are [most important]" as more than half the battle in building a teaching career that matters, tying the concept to long-term career sustainability.
quotes: But here's the thing that I understated with the group I was speaking to the other day: you satisfice many things so that you can maximize the living daylights out of a few really important things.
95% of the emails in my inbox merit a glance and then an archive. They need not be belabored. I need not formulate a pithy response to the group email thread.
My state's hyper-detailed teacher evaluation rubric is too much for my simple mind. I need not master it to master teaching.
I need not hyperventilate when there's an interruption to my lesson plan. An overhead announcement, a kerfuffle in the hallway, an emergency drill I didn't catch in the weekly memo

My point with satisficing - and Nobel-winner Herbert Simon's point, when he first coined the term in the 50s - is that not all things are equally important. Knowing which things are is more than half the battle in building a teaching career that matters.
